nameStory: Thunberg's Geranium honors Carl Peter Thunberg, an 18th-century Swedish botanist who studied plants in Japan and was one of the first Europeans to document this species. It's also called Japanese Geranium because it's native to East Asia, though it has quietly made its way into some New England landscapes. The name 'geranium' comes from the Greek word for crane, referring to the long, pointed seed pods that look like a crane's bill.
description: Thunberg's Geranium is a low-growing annual herb that spreads along the ground or forms small mounds up to about a foot tall. This delicate-looking plant produces small pink to white flowers with five rounded petals throughout much of the growing season. Its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves give it a lacy appearance, and like other geraniums, it develops the characteristic long-beaked seed pods that split dramatically when ripe. Though uncommon in New England, it's an interesting find for plant enthusiasts exploring disturbed areas or garden edges.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The distinctive long, pointed seed pods look exactly like a crane's bill and split explosively when ripe, launching seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' - this is the most reliable way to identify any true geranium

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small flowers about half an inch across with five rounded pink to white petals, often with darker pink veins, appearing singly or in pairs on slender stalks

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut, palm-shaped leaves divided into 3-5 narrow segments, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, arranged alternately along reddish stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that forms loose mats or small clumps, rarely exceeding 12 inches tall, with stems that often root where they touch the ground

habitat: Thunberg's Geranium is rarely encountered in New England but may be found in disturbed soils, garden edges, waste areas, and occasionally along roadsides or paths. It prefers partially shaded to sunny locations with moist, well-drained soil. When present, it's often mixed with other weedy or escaped garden plants in areas with some human disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants develop their characteristic deeply divided leaves. Early flowers may appear by late spring in warmer locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small pink to white flowers appearing continuously. This is the best time to spot the distinctive crane's-bill seed pods forming and splitting.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering until frost, with mature seed pods explosively dispersing seeds. Foliage may turn reddish before the plant dies back completely.
seasonality.winter: This annual plant dies completely, leaving no above-ground trace. Only seeds remain dormant in the soil until the following spring.

funFact: In Japan, this humble little plant is considered one of the most trusted folk medicines and is even an official pharmaceutical drug for treating diarrhea - so valued that its Japanese name 'ゲンノショウコ' literally means 'actual proof' because it works so reliably!
confusionNotes: The deeply divided leaves might be confused with other small geraniums, but the explosive seed pods are the giveaway for any true geranium. Don't confuse it with the showy garden 'geraniums' (which are actually Pelargoniums) - those have completely different flowers and thick, succulent stems that smell spicy when crushed.
contextualKnowledge: Like many plants called 'geraniums,' there's potential for confusion since the colorful garden plants most people call geraniums are actually in the genus Pelargonium. True geraniums like Thunberg's are in the genus Geranium and are typically more modest wildflowers with the distinctive crane's-bill seed pods that garden geraniums lack.
compareHints: Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers. Unlike the robust Herb Robert with its strong musky smell and red stems, Thunberg's Geranium is nearly scentless and has a gentler appearance. Its low, spreading growth habit also sets it apart from most other New England geraniums, which tend to grow more upright.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
